> **What this case shows** — free-living physical-activity analysis rests on one
> number: **ENMO**, the Euclidean-norm-minus-one acceleration. On real continuous
> accelerometer data the ecosystem's `computeENMO()` reproduces the field-standard
> **GGIR** implementation to **machine precision** — maximum difference **1.35 ×
> 10⁻¹⁴ g**, correlation **1.000000** over 749 epochs. On that exact foundation the
> free-living summary runs end to end: intensity time-use, the **Rowlands
> intensity gradient** (−1.19) and **activity fragmentation** (active-to-sedentary
> transition probability 0.11). **What reproduces, and what doesn't** — the ENMO
> reproduction is exact and transferable; the summary *metrics* are demonstrated
> on a real recording, but this recording is a scripted **protocol**, not a
> free-living day, so the absolute intensity numbers reflect the protocol and the
> ~1 h length makes MX metrics degenerate (not claimed). **How to read it** — left,
> our ENMO vs GGIR's on the line of identity; right, the intensity gradient — the
> log-log slope of time spent against acceleration intensity.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — turn raw acceleration into a physical-behaviour profile in three
moves: **compute ENMO** per epoch → **summarise** intensity time-use, the
intensity gradient and MX metrics → **quantify fragmentation** (how activity and
rest are accumulated).
**Way of thinking** — before trusting any downstream metric, verify the
*foundation*: does your ENMO match the reference implementation on the same
signal? Then read the intensity gradient (cut-point-free) rather than a single
MVPA threshold, and keep the recording length in mind — MX and gradient need a
full worn day to mean what the literature means.
**Ecosystem usage** — `computeENMO()` → `summarizeFreeLiving()` /
`intensityGradient()` (PhysioWearable); the same epoch series feeds every metric.
:::

## Proposition

`computeENMO()` reproduces GGIR to machine precision on real accelerometer data
(max difference **1.35 × 10⁻¹⁴ g**, correlation **1.000000**). On that foundation
the free-living summary computes the intensity gradient (**−1.19**), MVPA time and
activity fragmentation (ASTP **0.11**) end to end.

## Question & goal

**The question is one of foundations.** Free-living accelerometry has a de-facto
reference — **GGIR** (van Hees et al.) — and any new pipeline's first duty is to
match it on the metric everything is built from, ENMO. PAMAP2 (Reiss & Stricker
2012) provides real continuous 100 Hz accelerometer recordings; we take one
subject's hand sensor and ask: does `computeENMO()` reproduce GGIR's ENMO exactly,
and does the physical-behaviour summary then run on that foundation?

## Challenge & approach

The challenge is honesty about two different things. **Foundation**: ENMO must
match GGIR *exactly* — a bit-for-bit agreement, not "close". **Summary**: the
free-living metrics (intensity gradient, MX, fragmentation) are *designed for a
worn day*, and PAMAP2 is a lab protocol, so we compute them to demonstrate the
pipeline but scope their interpretation. We convert the hand accelerometer to g,
compute ENMO with both `computeENMO()` and `GGIR::g.applymetrics()` on the
identical signal, then run `summarizeFreeLiving()`.

## Data

**PAMAP2** subject101 hand IMU (Reiss & Stricker 2012, UCI #231) — ~1 h of
gap-free 100 Hz acceleration. Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![ENMO agreement, computeENMO vs GGIR, on the line of identity (left) and the
Rowlands intensity gradient — minutes vs intensity on log-log axes
(right).](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* on the left, every 5-second epoch's ENMO under our
implementation (y) against GGIR's (x) — they are indistinguishable. On the right,
the time spent falls log-linearly with intensity; the slope is the intensity
gradient, a cut-point-free summary of the whole intensity distribution.

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| ENMO max difference vs GGIR | **1.35 × 10⁻¹⁴ g** |
| ENMO correlation vs GGIR | **1.000000** |
| intensity gradient | −1.19 |
| MVPA minutes (over the recording) | 28.6 |
| activity→sedentary transition probability | 0.11 |

## Conclusion

The physical-activity foundation is exact: two independent implementations agree
to 10⁻¹⁴ g on real data, so a free-living pipeline built on `computeENMO()`
inherits GGIR's ENMO by construction. The higher-level summary runs end to end,
with the honest caveat that a lab protocol is not a free-living day. The
transferable takeaway: **validate the foundation metric against the reference
before trusting anything downstream — then read the intensity distribution, not a
single cut-point.**

## Open questions

- PAMAP2 is a lab protocol, so the intensity time-use is not a real-world day;
  the full free-living summary (MX metrics, a diurnal profile, guideline
  attainment) needs a genuinely free-living public recording. *Documented, not
  escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| step | function | package |
|---|---|---|
| compute ENMO per epoch | `computeENMO()` | PhysioWearable |
| free-living behaviour summary | `summarizeFreeLiving()` | PhysioWearable |
| intensity gradient / MX metrics | `intensityGradient()` / `mxMetrics()` | PhysioWearable |
| activity fragmentation | `activityFragmentation()` | PhysioWearable |

**Choosing the parameters:** 5-second epochs and the Hildebrand cut-points are the
GGIR defaults; auto-calibrate raw data first (`autoCalibrateAccel()`), require a
minimum wear day (≥10 h) before trusting a person's summary, and read the
intensity gradient alongside MVPA. Pair this with `adl-har-ucihar` (which activity)
and the ICF performance mapping (`freeLivingICF()`).

```r
library(PhysioWearable)
enmo <- computeENMO(accel, sampling_rate = 100, epoch_sec = 5, unit = "mg")
summarizeFreeLiving(enmo, epoch_sec = 5)         # time-use, gradient, MX, fragmentation
```

One line for the technical reader: every number traces to
[`artifacts/enmo_agreement.csv`](artifacts/enmo_agreement.csv) and
[`artifacts/freeliving_summary.csv`](artifacts/freeliving_summary.csv), re-checked
